raw_text:
The coronary slow flow phenomenon (CSFP) is an angiographic entity in which contrast opacification of the distal coronary tree is delayed despite absent or non-obstructive epicardial coronary disease. First described by Tambe and colleagues in 1972 [1], it became more reproducibly characterized after the corrected thrombolysis in myocardial infarction frame count (CTFC) was introduced by Gibson et al. [2]. Contemporary definitions generally require no obstructive stenosis—often <40% to 50% diameter narrowing—plus TIMI-2 flow or CTFC >27 frames, after exclusion of secondary causes such as coronary ectasia, spasm, embolization, acute reperfusion no-reflow, severe valvular disease, cardiomyopathy, hypotension, or technical injection factors [3-5].

CSFP is uncommon but not rare in catheterization laboratories. Prevalence estimates vary with referral population and criteria: early and contemporary cohorts report roughly 1% to 7% among patients undergoing angiography for suspected coronary disease [4,6]. Typical patients are middle-aged men, frequently smokers, and often have obesity, dyslipidemia or metabolic syndrome [6,7]. Clinically, CSFP should not be dismissed as a benign angiographic curiosity. It is associated with recurrent rest angina, abnormal stress tests, emergency presentations mimicking acute coronary syndrome, impaired quality of life and repeated angiography [4,8,9]. Serious events are uncommon but reported, including ventricular arrhythmias, QT-dispersion abnormalities, and sudden cardiac death [10,11].

Pathophysiology is heterogeneous. Histopathology has shown small-vessel wall thickening, luminal narrowing, endothelial edema and mitochondrial abnormalities, supporting a structural microvascular component [3]. Intravascular ultrasound and physiologic studies further suggest diffuse, angiographically “hidden” atherosclerosis, intimal thickening, calcification, and increased resting coronary microvascular resistance [12,13]. Importantly, preserved hyperemic coronary flow reserve in some patients indicates that CSFP is not synonymous with all forms of coronary microvascular dysfunction; rather, it may reflect increased basal tone or resting resistance with preserved vasodilator reserve in a subset [13]. Endothelial dysfunction is central: studies report impaired nitric-oxide bioavailability, increased endothelin-1, abnormal endothelial nitric oxide synthase responses, and disturbed vascular reactivity [14-16]. Platelet activation, inflammatory pathways, immune-cell indices and altered biomarkers also appear relevant [17-20]. Proteomic and genetic studies suggest additional mechanisms, but these remain hypothesis-generating [21,22].

Diagnosis rests on careful angiographic technique and objective frame counting. CTFC should be measured in at least one epicardial artery, correcting the LAD by 1.7; diffuse multivessel slowing suggests more extensive microvascular involvement. Because CSFP overlaps with ischemia and non-obstructive coronary arteries, vasospastic angina and microvascular angina, clinical interpretation should integrate symptoms, ECG changes, noninvasive ischemia testing, and—where available—coronary function testing. Recent data caution that visually assessed or angiographic slow flow alone is an imperfect surrogate for invasively defined coronary microvascular dysfunction, reinforcing the need for mechanism-based phenotyping in persistent angina [23].

Treatment evidence remains limited and mostly small-trial or observational. Acute intracoronary vasodilators may improve frame counts; diltiazem appears more effective than nitroglycerin in one randomized angiographic study [24]. Chronic calcium-channel blockade has the strongest clinical signal: oral diltiazem improved angina, exercise tolerance and coronary flow at 6 months, and mibefradil reduced angina and nitrate use in a crossover trial, although mibefradil is no longer widely available [25,26]. Nebivolol, nicorandil and statins have been associated with improved endothelial function, symptoms or perfusion markers in small studies [27-29]. More recently, endothelin-A antagonism with zibotentan reduced angina frequency in a pilot crossover trial, consistent with the endothelin hypothesis [30]. In practice, management should combine risk-factor modification—especially smoking cessation, lipid and metabolic control—with individualized antianginal therapy, while acknowledging the absence of large outcome trials.
